blocks.text: Leadership Isn't What It Used to Be

"I've spent years developing my skills and leadership instincts, but now everybody talks about AI like it's the future of work. Where does that leave me? Can AI make my judgment obsolete, or can it actually make me a better leader?" Does that sound familiar? Have you ever thought about something like that? Well, AI isn't here to replace your leadership — it's here to amplify it. To achieve this, you need to know how to work with it, and that's exactly what you're going to learn in this course!
The Control Problem

Traditional leadership was built on control. You directed tasks, monitored execution, and made decisions based on information that flowed up to you.

That model is breaking down, and the reason isn't that the leaders aren't capable. It's because the volume and complexity of decisions have exploded beyond what a single person can process alone.

feedbackCorrect.text: Time is the constraint, not information or authority. You're drowning in decisions that need your judgment, but you can't give each one the attention it deserves.

feedbackIncorrect.text: Most leaders have access to data and decision-making authority. The real bottleneck is cognitive bandwidth — there aren't enough hours to think through everything that lands on your desk.

options.label: Not having enough time to think deeply about strategic decisions
Not having access to the right data or information
Not having enough authority to make important calls

blocks.text: This is where the old leadership model fails. You can't solve a time problem by working harder or delegating more tasks to people. You need something that can process complexity at scale, surface insights you'd miss, and free up your cognitive bandwidth for the decisions that truly need human judgment. That's not about control anymore — it's about collaboration with intelligent systems.
From Directing to Orchestrating

Imagine conducting an orchestra. You don't play every instrument yourself. Instead, you set the vision and make the critical interpretive decisions, while each section handles its specialized work.

With AI, it's the same — you use different AI tools for different purposes and maximize your efficiency.

feedbackCorrect.text: AI excels at processing large volumes, generating options, and handling first drafts — all tasks that free up your time for higher-level thinking and human judgment calls.

feedbackIncorrect.text: AI can support decision-making with analysis, but decisions involving human judgment — like promotions, cultural fit, or ethical trade-offs — require your leadership intuition and values.

blocks.text: Meet Claude
Let's see how this works in practice with Claude — an AI assistant designed for complex thinking and analysis.

This tool works best when you treat it like a strategic thinking partner — someone you'd brainstorm with, test ideas against, or ask to analyze something from a different angle.

The key difference? Claude can process information at scale and respond instantly, but it still needs your direction, context, and judgment to be useful.

feedbackCorrect.text: While experimentation has value, understanding your role's structure first lets you strategically identify where AI can amplify your work and where you need to stay hands-on. This saves time and prevents misapplication.

feedbackIncorrect.text: Experimentation can work, but without a framework, you'll waste time testing AI on judgment-heavy tasks where it doesn't fit. Start by mapping your role, then apply AI strategically to the right areas.

blocks.text: Building Your AI Integration Roadmap
The audit gives you raw analysis, but now you need to turn it into something actionable — a simple roadmap that guides your daily AI use.
Your roadmap should answer three questions:

• What tasks do I delegate to AI?
  • What tasks do I keep entirely human-led?
  • What's my workflow for each AI-assisted task?
This turns abstract categories into concrete practices you can implement immediately.
Let's refine the audit results into a practical roadmap you can reference daily.

blocks.text: The Thinking Partner vs. Doing Engine Framework

Before moving forward, have you noticed Claude mentioning the thinking and doing zones?

Actually, these are the two main modes of using AI, and understanding the difference between them is very important.

• Thinking Partner: AI helps you think better — surfacing insights, testing assumptions, generating scenarios, and expanding your perspective before you make decisions.
  • Doing Engine: AI executes defined tasks — drafting documents, analyzing data, summarizing meetings, or formatting presentations based on clear instructions you provide.

Most leaders only use AI in Doing Engine mode — treating it like a faster assistant for tasks they've already decided to do.

The Blind Spot Problem

Think of a situation: you've spent weeks preparing your strategic plan for the board, but there's a nagging feeling: "What if I'm missing something?" Does that sound familiar? That's when you need someone to challenge your thinking, and AI can be exactly that. Let's learn more about it!

feedbackCorrect.text: When you've been working on something for weeks, your eyes can glaze over. You stop seeing flaws that would be obvious to someone fresh.

feedbackIncorrect.text: Data and time aren't the risk per se — perspective is. You need someone who'll push back on your thinking before you present to stakeholders who definitely will.

options.label: Missing critical flaws because you've been too close to the work

blocks.question: Let's start with a quick quiz: when preparing a major strategy, what's the biggest risk?

blocks.text:
Yes, it happens — when you're too close to your work, you can stop seeing the downsides. And asking your team to poke holes in something they helped create also may not produce honest criticism.

What you need is a skeptical outsider who'll challenge every assumption.
The Devil's Advocate You Need
Claude can be the valuable skeptical outsider you need!

feedbackCorrect.text: Claude is able to help you prepare by surfacing the tough questions before you're in the room. You're not looking for validation — you're looking for blind spots.

feedbackIncorrect.text: The goal isn't to prove you're right or replace your judgment. It's to find weaknesses while you still have time to fix them, and that's exactly what Claude can do.

options.label: It can stress-test assumptions you might be taking for granted
It can surface objections you can address before facing real stakeholders
It can make the final strategic decision for you
It can prove your strategy is correct
It can force you to think through counterarguments in advance

blocks.question: Given what you know about Claude, how do you think it could help you?

blocks.text: To see how this works in action, imagine you gave Claude your strategic plan and now want to analyze it objectively.

blocks.exampleResponse: I've reviewed your 2026 strategic plan. As a skeptical VC who's seen many expansion strategies struggle, here are my concerns: Top 5 Risks: — Market timing assumption: You're banking on Q2 demand, but economic indicators suggest customers may delay purchases. — Resource constraints: Scaling to 3 new markets simultaneously will stretch your operations team thin. — Competitive response overlooked: Your plan assumes competitors won't react to your market entry. — Cash flow gap: There's a 6-month period where expenses spike before revenue materializes. — Dependency on key hire: Success hinges on filling the VP of Sales role, but there's no backup plan. These aren't fatal, but each needs mitigation before I'd invest.

feedbackCorrect.text: The value isn't prediction — it's preparation. You now know which objections to anticipate and can strengthen those areas before facing real scrutiny.

feedbackIncorrect.text: Claude doesn't predict success. It surfaces questions skeptical stakeholders will ask, giving you time to prepare strong responses or adjust the plan.

blocks.question: Looking at this feedback, what makes it valuable for strategy preparation?

feedbackCorrect.text: By assigning Claude the role of "skeptical venture capitalist," you told it exactly which lens to use — someone who's cautious about expansion and has seen strategies fail before.

feedbackIncorrect.text: Claude needs direction. Without a specific role, it would give generic feedback. The "skeptical VC" framing shaped the entire analysis toward investment risk.

blocks.question: Why do you think Claude was able to give you a valuable output?

blocks.text: You can give Claude a role — a skeptical investor, a critical board member, a worried CFO — and it will challenge your thinking from that independent perspective. This is called strategic war-gaming: testing your strategy against different adversarial viewpoints before the real conversation happens. The key? Specific roles produce specific challenges.
blocks.title: 💡 Strategic War-Gaming With Roles

blocks.text: The more specific the role, the more useful the challenge. If you just ask to "be critical," it will most probably produce generic feedback. In turn, "Act as a CFO worried about cash flow" will definitely produce targeted financial scrutiny. Let's look at a couple more examples next!

feedbackCorrect.text: "Critic" could mean anything — a business critic, a design critic, a technical critic. Without a field or perspective, you're likely to get generic pushback instead of targeted challenges.

feedbackIncorrect.text: You need to tell Claude whose perspective to adopt — investor, customer, regulator, competitor — to get useful challenges.

feedbackCorrect.text: This tells Claude the stakeholder type (board member), their bias (risk-averse), and their experience (expansion failures). You'll get focused, relevant challenges.

feedbackIncorrect.text: The more context you give about the stakeholder's perspective, the more useful the challenge.

Building on the war-gaming concept, this is how you can develop strong adversarial roles:
  • Stakeholder type: investor, board member, customer, regulator

The Meeting You Missed

You're triple-booked. The weekly sync with the engineering team went on without you, and now you need to know: did they commit to the new deadline?

Normally, you'd ask someone for notes or spend 30 minutes scrubbing through a recording. With AI, you get the answer in 10 seconds.
The Lost Intelligence Problem

Every meeting contains decisions, commitments, and context. 

But most of that intelligence disappears the moment the call ends because people take incomplete notes, key decisions get buried in recordings, and commitments never get documented.
AI meeting tools solve this by creating searchable records of every conversation.

feedbackIncorrect.text: AI doesn't decide meeting importance — that's your judgment. What it does is make meeting content instantly accessible and searchable when you need it.

blocks.question: How could AI-powered meeting intelligence help leaders who can't attend every meeting?

blocks.text: Setting Up Meeting Intelligence
The tool you use depends on your organization's platform. This is how to enable automatic recording and transcription for both.
For Google Meet Users
If your team uses Google Meet, you can use Gemini to capture and summarize meetings.
For Microsoft Teams Users
If your team uses Microsoft Teams, you'll most likely use Microsoft Copilot.
Setting Up and Accessing Transcripts
For Google Meet:

1. Go to Settings → Meeting records
  2. Check the "Take notes with Gemini" and "Transcribe the meeting" features
  3. When you enter a meeting, transcribing starts automatically.
After meeting:

1. Go to the "Meet Recordings" folder in Google Drive.
  2. Open transcript (appears as a Google Doc). It's ready to be processed with Gemini!
For Microsoft Teams:

1. Click "More actions" (...)
  2. Select "Start recording," and transcription will start automatically too.
After meeting:

1. Look into the "Recap" section of the meeting after opening it in the calendar.
  2. View transcript and AI-generated summary. Copilot automatically highlights key points!
Querying Meetings for Specific Answers
Once you access the recordings, you can ask specific questions and get targeted answers without re-listening.
Let's go back to the engineering sync that you missed. Imagine you got the Gemini transcript, and now need to know if they committed to the revised launch date.

blocks.exampleResponse: Yes, the engineering team committed to the new deadline. Here's what was said: [Timestamp: 34:12] Engineering Lead: "We can hit March 15th if we deprioritize the admin dashboard redesign." [Timestamp: 34:45] Project Manager: "Confirmed — March 15th is the new target date." Decision: March 15th launch date, contingent on deprioritizing the admin dashboard.

Say you need to catch up on the quarterly planning discussion without having to listen to an hour-long recording.

blocks.text: The Last-Minute Deck Problem

It's 2 p.m. Your presentation to the C-suite is in two hours. You have the data, strategy, and insights, but you're still not ready. You don't have the slides. Does that sound familiar? This is where AI transforms panic into polish. Let's see how!
The Blank Slide Problem

If you create a presentation the traditional way, you start from scratch.

An hour later, you're still fiddling with layouts, searching for stock images, and trying to make charts that don't look embarrassing.

But presentations aren't only about making pretty slides — they're about communicating strategy clearly under time pressure.

You need something that handles the visual work while you focus on the narrative.

feedbackCorrect.text: AI excels at visual execution — layouts, charts, themes. It transforms your content into structured slides, leaving you time to refine the narrative and strategic emphasis.

feedbackIncorrect.text: Strategic decisions about what matters to your audience require your judgment. AI handles the visual heavy lifting so you can focus on the story and message.

blocks.text: Meet Beautiful.ai
Beautiful.ai is an AI-powered presentation tool designed specifically for these tasks:

• You give it your rough structure and key points.
  • It generates a complete presentation with layouts, visuals, and design consistency.
To see this in action, imagine you're a Sales Director who needs to present a Q3 Pipeline Review to the C-suite in one hour.
You have these notes scattered across documents:

• Current pipeline value: $4.2M
  • Top 3 deals in the final stages
  • New lead sources that are performing well
  • One major deal at risk
Instead of copy-pasting these into slide templates one by one, you'll feed them to Beautiful.ai and let it draft populated slides — data, framing, and layout in one pass.

blocks.text:
Beautiful.ai drafted a 10-slide deck with your data already in place — pipeline value on the opener, top deals on their own slide, and the at-risk deal flagged.

But when you scroll through it, most slides are heavy on bullet points. Beautiful.ai used what you gave it, and you didn't tell it where a visual would land better than text.

The pattern for fast presentation generation:
  • List your key sections (3-6 main points).
  • Specify the theme/tone (professional, creative, technical).
  • Let AI generate structure and layouts.
  • Spend your time refining content and narrative.

blocks.question: When you need to write an important message, what takes the most time?

blocks.text: When "Good" Isn't Good Enough
If you've prompted Claude to draft an important message, you might have noticed something: the draft is thorough, thoughtful, well-structured. And it still doesn't sound like you.
The problem isn't that AI can't write. It writes well by default — thoroughly, carefully, and professionally. But "well" isn't the same as "in your voice.”

blocks.text: There's a second cost to sending a message like this as-is. Overpolished writing has become a tell — readers increasingly recognize it as AI-generated, and in professional contexts, that shifts how they read you. A message meant to feel human starts to feel outsourced.

The fix isn't writing everything yourself. You can teach Claude how you write, so its drafts start from your voice — not a polished-but-anonymous default.

Once Claude knows your style, drafting shifts from hours to minutes, and the output actually sounds like it came from you.
The process is simple:

1. Give Claude 2-3 examples of your writing in a specific tone (e.g., empathetic, direct, or celebratory).
  2. Ask it to match that style in new communications.
Claude will learn your patterns — how you open messages, how you explain things, how you balance different elements.

blocks.text: When "Good" Isn't Good Enough
If you've prompted Claude to draft an important message, you might have noticed something: the draft is thorough, thoughtful, well-structured. And it still doesn't sound like you.
The problem isn't that AI can't write. It writes well by default — thoroughly, carefully, and professionally. But "well" isn't the same as "in your voice.”

Leading AI Responsibly

Throughout this guide, you've seen how AI accelerates research, communication, presentations, meetings, and data analysis.

But with this power comes significant risk — and without the right guardrails, AI adoption can create problems far worse than the inefficiencies it solves.
The Governance Gap
Imagine this:

• Your engineering team is pasting client code into ChatGPT to debug faster.
  • Your sales team is uploading prospect lists to analyze patterns.
Both think they're being productive.

However, they're actually creating massive security risks — and you don't have a policy to stop them.

AI adoption without governance is like handing out company credit cards without spending limits.

feedbackCorrect.text: The real risk is security. Without governance, well-meaning employees will paste passwords, client data, and proprietary information into public tools.

feedbackIncorrect.text: Experimentation and competitive pace matter, but security breaches and compliance violations can destroy organizations. Governance protects against catastrophic risk.

options.label: Employees unknowingly expose sensitive data through external AI tools
The organization falls behind competitors in AI capabilities

blocks.question: What could be the biggest risk of AI adoption without clear policies?

blocks.text: Keeping this in mind, leadership's job isn't to block AI. I's to create clear, accessible policies that enable safe use.
Building AI Guardrails
So, let's establish approval processes and make guidelines easy to follow.
We'll use Notion to create a living policy document and reference wiki that your team can actually use.
Drafting Your AI Use Policy

Start by using Notion AI to generate the initial structure. 

This gives you a framework to refine rather than starting from scratch.

blocks.text:
This structure provides the foundation. 

You can then refine it to match your organization's specific risks and context.
Creating a Red/Yellow/Green Tool Framework
Once your structure is ready, the next step is to tell people which tools are safe for what types of data. They need concrete guidance.

The key point here is that not all AI tools handle data the same way. The difference: whether the tool uses your inputs for training. For example, free versions of ChatGPT, Claude, and similar tools may use your prompts to improve their models. This means sensitive data could appear in responses to other users.

In turn, enterprise contracts change this. Tools like ChatGPT Enterprise, Claude for Enterprise, or Gemini for Business explicitly guarantee your data won't be used for training.

This distinction determines what's safe: free tools work for public content, but sensitive data requires enterprise-grade privacy protections.

feedbackCorrect.text: Usability comes from specificity and accessibility. People need quick answers: "Can I use this tool for this task?" Legal comprehensiveness doesn't help decision-making in the moment.

feedbackIncorrect.text: Legal language protects the organization, but doesn't help employees make real-time decisions. Effective governance is clear, specific, and immediately actionable.

options.label: Detailed legal language covering all potential scenarios
Accessible reference documentation teams can check in the moment
Clear categories that help people self-assess risk quickly
Specific examples of what data can go into which tools

  • Client personal information, passwords, proprietary code with identifiers
  • Why: Exposure could cause legal/compliance violations
Yellow Zone — Sanitized Data Only:
  • Internal strategy documents (remove names/numbers first)
  • Meeting notes (strip confidential details before uploading)
  • Why: Safe after removing identifying information
Green Zone — Open AI Use Allowed:
  • Public marketing copy, blog posts, general research questions
  • Why: Already public or non-sensitive content

Identifying AI Risk Areas
Beyond data security, leaders must also consider where AI introduces bias or undermines critical judgment.

feedbackCorrect.text: These are high-stakes human decisions where bias, context, and judgment are critical. AI can inform, but humans must decide and remain accountable.

feedbackIncorrect.text: Administrative tasks like scheduling don't require human judgment at every step. The risk areas are where AI could perpetuate bias or make consequential errors affecting people's lives.

options.label: Hiring, promotion, or termination decisions
Legal compliance determinations
Performance evaluations and compensation changes
Scheduling meetings or managing calendar logistics

blocks.question: In which scenarios should AI never be the sole decision-maker?

blocks.text:
AI governance works only when it is anchored in clear moments where human judgment steps in. In practice, this means AI can surface insights while people remain the ones who make the final calls. 

Every AI-generated output still goes through human review, and experts retain the authority to override any recommendation the system produces.

Ultimately, accountability never shifts — a real person is responsible for each decision made with AI's help.

blocks.text: Making Governance Accessible

The last step is to make your policy work.

But when does it work? When it's visible to the team!

feedbackCorrect.text: Accessibility drives compliance. When people can instantly check "Is this safe?" they'll follow guidelines. Barriers create workarounds.

feedbackIncorrect.text: Training and monitoring have roles, but compliance comes from making the right choice the easy choice. If checking the policy takes 30 seconds, people will use it.

Require mandatory training and signed acknowledgment forms
Make policies accessible as a searchable wiki, so teams can check instantly

blocks.text: Leading AI Responsibly

Throughout this guide, you've seen how AI accelerates research, communication, presentations, meetings, and data analysis.

But with this power comes significant risk — and without the right guardrails, AI adoption can create problems far worse than the inefficiencies it solves.
The Governance Gap
Imagine this:

• Your engineering team is pasting client code into ChatGPT to debug faster.
  • Your sales team is uploading prospect lists to analyze patterns.
Both think they're being productive.

However, they're actually creating massive security risks — and you don't have a policy to stop them.

AI adoption without governance is like handing out company credit cards without spending limits.

feedbackCorrect.text: The real risk is security. Without governance, well-meaning employees will paste passwords, client data, and proprietary information into public tools.

feedbackIncorrect.text: Experimentation and competitive pace matter, but security breaches and compliance violations can destroy organizations. Governance protects against catastrophic risk.

options.label: Employees unknowingly expose sensitive data through external AI tools
The organization falls behind competitors in AI capabilities
Teams waste time experimenting with too many different tools

blocks.question: What could be the biggest risk of AI adoption without clear policies?

blocks.text: Keeping this in mind, leadership's job isn't to block AI. I's to create clear, accessible policies that enable safe use.
Building AI Guardrails
So, let's establish approval processes and make guidelines easy to follow.
We'll use Notion to create a living policy document and reference wiki that your team can actually use.
Drafting Your AI Use Policy

Start by using Notion AI to generate the initial structure. 

This gives you a framework to refine rather than starting from scratch.

blocks.prompt: Use Notion AI to draft the foundation of your responsible AI policy.
blocks.template: Draft [policy name] for [company industry]. Include sections on [security topic], [restrictions topic], and [review topic].

blocks.text:
This structure provides the foundation. 

You can then refine it to match your organization's specific risks and context.
Creating a Red/Yellow/Green Tool Framework
Once your structure is ready, the next step is to tell people which tools are safe for what types of data. They need concrete guidance.

The key point here is that not all AI tools handle data the same way. The difference: whether the tool uses your inputs for training. For example, free versions of ChatGPT, Claude, and similar tools may use your prompts to improve their models. This means sensitive data could appear in responses to other users.

In turn, enterprise contracts change this. Tools like ChatGPT Enterprise, Claude for Enterprise, or Gemini for Business explicitly guarantee your data won't be used for training.

This distinction determines what's safe: free tools work for public content, but sensitive data requires enterprise-grade privacy protections.

feedbackCorrect.text: Usability comes from specificity and accessibility. People need quick answers: "Can I use this tool for this task?" Legal comprehensiveness doesn't help decision-making in the moment.

feedbackIncorrect.text: Legal language protects the organization, but doesn't help employees make real-time decisions. Effective governance is clear, specific, and immediately actionable.

options.label: Detailed legal language covering all potential scenarios
Accessible reference documentation teams can check in the moment
Clear categories that help people self-assess risk quickly
Specific examples of what data can go into which tools

blocks.question: With all that in mind, what do you think will make an AI governance framework actually usable for teams?

blocks.text: So, the Red/Yellow/Green model provides instant clarity by categorizing data sensitivity and appropriate tools. To implement this idea, create a Notion database to categorize tools and data types.

How you can structure your reference database in Notion: Red Zone — Never Use External AI:
  • Client personal information, passwords, proprietary code with identifiers
  • Why: Exposure could cause legal/compliance violations
Yellow Zone — Sanitized Data Only:
  • Internal strategy documents (remove names/numbers first)
  • Meeting notes (strip confidential details before uploading)
  • Why: Safe after removing identifying information
Green Zone — Open AI Use Allowed:
  • Public marketing copy, blog posts, general research questions
  • Why: Already public or non-sensitive content
blocks.title: The Red/Yellow/Green Framework

blocks.text: Then add approved tools to each category. For example:

• Red: No external AI tools
  • Yellow: ChatGPT, Claude (with data sanitization)
  • Green: ChatGPT, Claude, Perplexity, public AI tools
Identifying AI Risk Areas
Beyond data security, leaders must also consider where AI introduces bias or undermines critical judgment.

feedbackCorrect.text: These are high-stakes human decisions where bias, context, and judgment are critical. AI can inform, but humans must decide and remain accountable.

feedbackIncorrect.text: Administrative tasks like scheduling don't require human judgment at every step. The risk areas are where AI could perpetuate bias or make consequential errors affecting people's lives.

options.label: Hiring, promotion, or termination decisions
Legal compliance determinations
Performance evaluations and compensation changes
Scheduling meetings or managing calendar logistics

blocks.question: In which scenarios should AI never be the sole decision-maker?

blocks.text:
AI governance works only when it is anchored in clear moments where human judgment steps in. In practice, this means AI can surface insights while people remain the ones who make the final calls. 

Every AI-generated output still goes through human review, and experts retain the authority to override any recommendation the system produces.

Ultimately, accountability never shifts — a real person is responsible for each decision made with AI's help.
blocks.title: 💡 Human-in-the-Loop

blocks.text: Making Governance Accessible

The last step is to make your policy work.

But when does it work? When it's visible to the team!

feedbackCorrect.text: Accessibility drives compliance. When people can instantly check "Is this safe?" they'll follow guidelines. Barriers create workarounds.

feedbackIncorrect.text: Training and monitoring have roles, but compliance comes from making the right choice the easy choice. If checking the policy takes 30 seconds, people will use it.

options.label: Implement monitoring software that flags policy violations
Require mandatory training and signed acknowledgment forms
Make policies accessible as a searchable wiki, so teams can check instantly
